Jeer

/jeer/ — rhymes with beer · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To jeer at someone is to mock or taunt them rudely, often as part of a crowd.

A few rude fans jeered at the rookie after his missed catch.

Worked Example

The rowdy fans jeered loudly when the quarterback threw an interception.

Jeer is more than simple mockery—it captures a crowd expressing public contempt, deliberately taunting someone to wound or belittle them. The word's power lies in its group element and hostile intent; plain 'mock' doesn't convey that vicious, collective mockery.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

mock: to make cruel fun of someone

taunt: to hurl insults meant to sting someone

sneer: to show scorn with a curled lip

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cheer: to shout approval, praise, and encouragement

applaud: to show enthusiastic approval by clapping

Where it sits · how loud and public the scorn — laugh at → mock → jeer → heckle

laugh at vs. jeer: Laugh at is much weaker than jeer: laughing at someone can be a passing giggle, while jeering means loudly hurling rude taunts, often with a whole crowd.

mock vs. jeer: Mock is weaker than jeer — mocking makes unkind fun of someone, but jeering shouts that mockery out loud and in public.

heckle vs. jeer: Heckle is stronger than jeer: a jeering crowd shouts scorn from the stands, while a heckler fires relentless, targeted interruptions to derail a speaker completely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — jeer

Root — jeer: to mock loudly, to roar mockingly (uncertain — possibly Dutch gieren ('to roar with laughter'))

Put it together

Put it together: Jeer arrived in English as a single, indivisible word in the 1550s, and even the experts aren't sure where it came from — perhaps a Dutch word for roaring with laughter, or a mocking twist on cheer. Its meaning has stayed steady ever since: loud, rude scorn aimed at someone, often by a crowd.

Use the root in a new word: cheer

Use the root in a new word: cheer: Some word historians think jeer may have begun as a mocking, upside-down use of cheer — a cheer shouts praise at a player, while a jeer flips it into an insult.

Strength Check

Word Choice

informal

Jeer describes intense, public, hostile mockery by a group. Use it when a crowd is deliberately taunting someone to wound them. For mild teasing or one-on-one criticism, 'mock' is a simpler, more neutral choice.
